analysis.one_liner: Slashes the capital gains tax rate to 5% for assets bought in 2021 and held over five years.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing or vote, dying with a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut the capital gains tax rate from 15-20% down to 5% on the sale of any property bought during 2021 and held for more than five years. That mostly benefits people who own large appreciated assets — stocks, real estate, business stakes — because the tax saved scales with the size of the gain. The bill was referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who bought assets in 2021 and hold them past five years. The savings grow with the size of the gain, so the largest benefits go to households with the biggest investment portfolios — someone selling $50,000 in appreciated stock saves a few thousand dollars, while someone selling $5 million saves hundreds of thousands.

how_it_helps.text: Reduces the capital gains rate to 5% (from the existing 15% or 20%) for any property purchased after December 31, 2020 and before January 1, 2022, once it has been held more than five years [S2][S3].

The benefit applies to the full sale of qualifying property, so the dollar savings scale directly with how much appreciated value the investor is selling — the larger the portfolio, the larger the tax cut [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, meaning taxpayers generally, since a lower rate on investment gains means less revenue unless the cut is paid for elsewhere. The bill contains no offsetting revenue provision [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill provides no offsetting revenue, so the lower rate adds to the deficit or must be paid for by other taxpayers [S3].

The benefit is concentrated: only people with taxable capital gains on assets bought in 2021 and held five-plus years qualify, and the savings scale with the size of the gain, so households with large investment portfolios capture most of the value [S3].
Long-term capital gains already carry a lower rate than wages; this would have widened the gap further, increasing the advantage of investment income over paycheck income [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people who qualify, the tax cut is real and substantial. But the design concentrates the benefit among the largest asset holders, and the bill includes no way to pay for the lost revenue, so the cost is spread across everyone who pays federal taxes. An honest backer would acknowledge this is a targeted rate cut for investors, not a broad tax relief measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Schweikert introduced the Invest Now Act on January 28, 2021, with Rep. Devin Nunes as its sole cosponsor [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; that was the only action ever taken on it [S5].
The Ways and Means Committee held no markup and the full House never voted on the bill before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one won anything concrete — the bill simply died without action. Investors with large portfolios would have gained the most had it passed; because it died, the Treasury kept the revenue, and taxpayers generally avoided the cost.

for.name: Rep. David Schweikert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a 5% capital gains rate for property bought in 2021 and held more than five years.

for.name: Rep. Devin Nunes
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other member signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never scheduled a markup or sent it to the floor, so it died at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee never advanced the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have cut the tax rate on gains from qualifying assets to 5%, with savings scaling to the size of the gain — a direct transfer of federal revenue to the households with the largest appreciated portfolios.

industries.industry: Private equity and venture capital funds
industries.note: Fund investors selling stakes bought in 2021 and held five-plus years would have paid 5% instead of 15-20% on their carried gains, a large reduction for large exits.
